title: Lark's Quiet Familiar
markdown:
Up where clouds tickled the mountain tops and wind whispered through tall pines, lived Lark. Not a cackling sort. Her potions smelled of blueberry muffins; her spells left shirts ironed and socks mysteriously un-lost. Clever, quirky, practical, a twinkle, a smudge of moon-dust on her nose. Her dearest friend: Tansy, a cat black as midnight, emerald eyes, Lark’s shadow and silent ear.

Cliffhaven, a cozy nest beneath rocky cliffs, buzzed: the Great Familiar Choosing, tradition old as the mountains. Lark, usually calm, felt a flutter. She needed a new familiar for witchy work. Stories of helpers who whispered on the wind or granted wishes with a tail-flick. Finding the right one felt as heavy as her oldest spellbook.

“Alright, Tansy.” Spectacles up: polished oak, lenses of captured starlight. “The market. Elder Grimble said it’s a super day for choosing. The sky-gems are lined up just right for the brave and the bonded.” A giggle like rustling leaves.

Tansy blinked slowly. High-country air, thin, crisp, pine and faraway snow. Tansy proud on Lark’s shoulder, black fur against blue robe, they started down toward the cliffside market. Tough mountain flowers pushed through rocks, bright petals like cheerful paint.

The market spread across a huge sloped hillside, a burst of colour against the grey rocks. Banners of red, blue, green, and yellow snapped like happy flags waving at the sky. Stalls piled high with shiny silks from silkworms that ate moonlight, tinkling trinkets that sang forgotten songs, magical herbs smelling of sunshine and dew, and creatures of all shapes trying to get noticed. The air buzzed with voices, hammers on magic metal, the occasional squawk. Nearby, bottled laughter jingled in little glass jars. Another stall offered cloud-fluff soft as dreams. It was all wonderfully, delightfully confusing, and Lark’s oldest spellbook, for once, had no index for this.

Lark frowned, thoughtful. “So many choices. Like picking one star from a whole sky.”

She saw a stall of glowing mushrooms that pulsed with soft light, making the merchant’s face look magical. Next to it, a man with a beard like a fluffy dandelion tried to sell giggling mushrooms; every time someone came near they burst into tiny bubbly giggles, and the merchant beamed. Further on, a creature like a fuzzy teapot with many legs puffed steam that smelled of cinnamon and warm cookies. Very cute. Lark guessed it was mostly good for a cozy cup of tea, which she already knew how to brew.

“Maybe a familiar should be quiet. Not prone to giggles. Or serving toast before the sun is up.” She stroked Tansy’s silk.

A rustle from shade under bottled starlight, tiny galaxies swirling. Out popped a small quick goblin, twitching ears, shirt patched with moss and leaves. Cricket: tricks, old stories, ancient rules, appearing from nowhere like a cheerful shadow.

“Ah, Witch Lark!” Pebbles in a can. “Looking for a familiar? Great quest! The air is bursting with possibilities!”

“Tricky, Cricket. Elder Grimble says we must choose the one that calls to the heart with the echo of old times, according to the Third Rule of the Whispering Pines.” The familiar confusing feeling of Grimble’s pronouncements.

Cricket rubbed a pointy chin, berry-juice fingers. “The Third Rule! Very special.” A wink. “Though nobody quite remembers what it is, or why it’s about familiars. Elder Grimble says follow it. Tradition!” He pointed at a tiny shiny dragon with butterfly wings. “Relative of the ancient Sky-Serpents, they say.”

Lark sighed. “So I pick a creature matching a rule no one understands, from a market of every creature except one that clearly calls to me.” She waved at a small fluffy cloud with wobbly eyes, floating, sometimes bumping a banner. “Nice. I bet its main skill is napping. I already have a perfectly good napper.” A scratch behind Tansy’s ears.

Tansy, who had watched the busy scene with calm, hopped down, paws hardly a sound. Smooth grace, ancient cat wisdom, toward a small simple pen in the corner. Inside, a rather plain dormouse nibbled a tiny seed, whiskers busy, a tiny straw hat looking very smart.

Tansy meowed, kind, a gentle rumble Lark felt. “The dormouse looks quite… like you.”

Lark blinked. “So tiny. Not scary at all. Elder Grimble said worthy of the old pacts.” She had imagined glowing horns, a cloak of stars.

Cricket popped up. “Worthy! A phoenix, a griffin? Or at least more than four legs and a roar that shakes mountains!” Chest puffed.

Lark watched the dormouse yawn, pink tongue, then clean its whiskers. No big glow. No announcement. Quiet, simple, happy in its small world. Still—

A gentle pull, not a loud call to adventure: a soft whisper in the mind, a shared quiet like sitting with Tansy by the fireplace on a rainy night, rain pattering, Tansy’s head on Lark’s lap, worries chased without a speech. Belonging. The market’s roar thinned around that one small pen.

“You know, Tansy.” Worries melting like snow in spring. “You’re absolutely right. Not big pronouncements. Not confusing rules from old stories. Connection.”

She knelt, robe rustling, offered a finger. The dormouse sniffed, tiny nose, a small polite nibble, whiskers tickling. Lark’s real warm smile.

“I choose you,” she whispered, and a soft golden light glowed from the tiny creature—not flashy, wonderfully warm. Then Tansy, eyes shining. “And I choose you, Tansy. Always.”

Cricket clapped, scattered acorns. “The dormouse it is! And the cat too! Unusual agreement, unusual witch!” Another wink, vanished toward shiny things.

Lark scooped the dormouse; it curled in her hand, tiny heart, solid and real. Tansy flicked a tail almost a dance, rubbed Lark’s leg, purring loud, filling the space where market-noise had been. They walked away from the busy market, banners still flapping a rainbow caught in the wind. Lark held the dormouse with care. It was no longer just a dormouse, but a reminder of quiet knowing. Tansy walked beside, a sleek shadow of loyalty, the perfect proof that the loudest stall had not been the point. Grimble could keep the Third Rule; Cricket could keep the Sky-Serpents. The hat, Lark thought, was the only ceremony required, and Tansy’s purr filled the path all the way to the first pine.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
